extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of experimental science, philosophers of science, and researchers learning methods of induction and causal inference
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the four principal methods of direct experimental induction (Method of Agreement, Method of Difference, Method of Concomitant Variations, Method of Residues), their proper application, limitations, and how deduction and experiment corroborate inductive conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances in which the effect occurs are compared to discover what antecedent they all share; that common antecedent is taken as evidence of a cause or causal factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when multiple diverse instances share the same consequent; if all instances that exhibit the effect have one antecedent in common, that antecedent (or something influencing it) may be one of the causes. Examples: Liebig's induction about metallic poisons (all poisonous cases involve formation of a compound resistant to putrefaction); induced electricity (opposite electricity found near charged conductors). Limitations: Agreement alone cannot distinguish cause from effect or rule out a common underlying cause; must be supplemented by other methods to establish causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare an instance where the effect occurs with an instance that is as similar as possible except for the absence of a single antecedent; if the effect is absent where that antecedent is absent, the antecedent is implicated as a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires that the positive and negative instances agree in all respects except one circumstance (or substance). Examples: antidotes to poisons (peroxide of iron checks arsenious acid); Leyden jar discharging shows paired opposite charges. Strict application is rigorous but often hard to attain because substances/cases differ in many properties; where exact isolation of one differing circumstance is not possible, seek multiple contrasting instances or indirect/deductive support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Causation is inferred from a correspondence in the magnitudes of variations: if changes in one variable are accompanied by proportional changes in another, the former may be (part of) the cause of the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when the antecedent and consequent vary together in degree rather than presence/absence. Examples: Leyden jar capacity and neighboring body's capacity limit charge; dew deposition correlates with conductivity, radiation, and texture (scales of intensity). Limitation: When observed variations are within narrow limits, very different laws may produce similar numerical results, risking incorrect extrapolation beyond observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for known parts of a phenomenon by known causes, and attribute the remaining unexplained part (the residue) to some other cause(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among methods of direct observation though not independent of deduction: it requires specific experience and deductive separation of accounted-for effects from residual effects. Use when complex phenomena have components already explained; the residue points to further causal factors. (Note: this chapter remarks that the Method of Residues is not independent of deduction.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference / Joint Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: When strict Method of Difference conditions cannot be met, combine many agreements and differences across varied instances to approximate the isolating power of strict difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when you cannot produce two instances identical except for one circumstance; instead, collect many instances showing agreement in a proposed causal property and many counterinstances lacking it. Example: multiple different antidotes all share the property of forming insoluble compounds with poisons—this joint evidence approaches the rigor of Method of Difference. Beware that this is weaker than a perfect difference-case, but can approach its certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the Phenomenon Precisely Before Inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly delimit and define the specific phenomenon to be investigated to ensure that the instances collected are genuinely comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary operation: separate dew from rain, fog moisture, etc.; only by precise definition can subsequent applications of Agreement, Difference, and Concomitant Variations be valid. Use measurements or operational criteria (e.g., thermometer tests for dew) to ensure cases are comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Deduction to Corroborate and Complete Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive reasoning from known laws can corroborate inductive inferences, demonstrate causation, and reveal additional necessary conditions or exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deduction from laws of aqueous vapor and heat shows why colder surfaces cause condensation and explains exceptions (dry air). Deduction can both prove causation and detect further conditions that observational methods might miss; it complements direct induction and strengthens conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Confirmation by Controlled Tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Where feasible, directly manipulate conditions to produce or prevent the effect and observe outcomes, fulfilling the Method of Difference experimentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cooling a surface to find the temperature at which dew forms; administering antidotes and observing whether poisoning is prevented. Even small-scale experiments help confirm causation; natural 'experiments' (e.g., cloud clearing causing dew) can also satisfy Method of Difference if they introduce a single definite change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of Extrapolation Beyond Observed Limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions valid within observed ranges may fail beyond those limits because different numerical laws can agree closely within narrow ranges yet diverge outside them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observed variations are small relative to possible ranges, very different laws may produce similar results within observation limits (examples: empirical formulae for elasticity of steam, resistance of fluids failing beyond original range). Be cautious applying a deduced numerical law outside the domain of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to Examine Negative Cases and Counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain causation one must seek instances where the effect is absent and examine which antecedents are absent in those cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative instances are essential for the Method of Difference. Examples: insoluble basic salts of arsenic are non-poisonous; nitrate of silver is caustic externally but not poisonous orally because stomach chemistry converts it to an insoluble form. Use negative cases to eliminate candidate antecedents and strengthen causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Alternative Properties and Confounding Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that substances and instances possess many properties; do not assume a single identified property is causal without excluding other possible properties or modes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an antidote might counteract a poison by some property other than forming an insoluble compound; therefore, to support causation, find multiple substances that act as antidotes and share only the hypothesized property. Always consider and test for other plausible mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement Alone Does Not Establish Direction of Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when two phenomena invariably coincide, Agreement cannot determine which is cause and which is effect (or if both result from a common cause) without further methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: observation that objects that take dew are colder than air shows association; only by applying Difference, Concomitant Variations, or Deduction (showing surface coldness arises independently) can one conclude that coldness causes dew rather than the reverse. Use supplementary methods to resolve directionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine Multiple Methods to Increase Certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The four inductive methods, used together with deduction and properly designed experiments, compose the available resources for ascertaining causal laws and increase confidence in conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter emphasizes that Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues, and Deduction together (and in sequence where appropriate) produce stronger, more reliable inductions than any single method alone. Use examples (poisons, electricity, dew) as models for integrating methods in investigation.
